title: WISE 0855−0714 (coldest known brown dwarf)
astrometry_source: Position: AllWISE designation 08h55m10.831s -07d14m42.53s as given in the challenge (epoch assumed 2010.5). Motion: Luhman & Esplin 2016 (AJ 152, 78) as transcribed by the Y Dwarf Compendium; not checked against the paper.

story.hook: The coldest brown dwarf known, 7 light-years away. A faint dot creeps west — but watch out for its neighbour.
story.what_to_look_for: Pick D5 (3.8–4.4 µm) or D6 (4.4–5.0 µm), where cold brown dwarfs glow, and blink the first and last visit. A faint dot inside the blue circle shifts to the right (west) by about one pixel per year. Then switch to D1 or D2: the light you see near the circle there comes from a different, ordinary star 7.8 arcseconds away that does not move. Tip: the challenge's coordinates are from 2010; since then WISE 0855 has moved about 2 arcminutes west, which is why the circle is not at the old position.
story.what_it_is: WISE 0855−0714 is a brown dwarf about 7 light-years away, roughly as cold as Earth's North Pole in winter. It was found in 2014 because it moves fast across the sky in WISE images (about 8 arcseconds per year). It is almost invisible at short infrared wavelengths and gives off most of its light near 4.5 µm.
story.answer: WISE 0855 is the faint dot in the circle in the 3.8–5 µm bands; it shifts west by about 1.3 pixels per year. The steady star just beside it is an unrelated Gaia star (G = 16.3).
story.honest: This is near the limit of SPHEREx. In the 3.8–5 µm bands, a faint source sits within about half a pixel of the predicted position and shifts west between visits by about the predicted amount. That is consistent with SPHEREx seeing WISE 0855, but we have not proven it: a background star 7.8 arcseconds away blends with it, and the signal in single frames is weak. At 0.75–3.8 µm the light at the circle is mostly that background star. For the same reason, its brightness chart is not reliable: the measuring circle includes part of the neighbouring star.
